rationale: The book's identification of 'heart of the earth' as Jerusalem (navel/center of the land) is carried by the explicit OT localizations in Ezekiel, the precise linguistic mirror to Jonah's 'heart of the seas,' and the consistent symbolic method that already defines sea as peoples and ship as political body. This accounts for the full Jonah narrative as the sign (not a truncated duration comparison), dissolves the three-days-and-nights counting problem without calendar special pleading, and fits every supplied detail of arrest-custody-death-release better than the tomb/Hades reading. The traditional alternative, while consensus, rests on surface synonymy that Scripture never states and that creates the very chronological difficulty the book removes; its supporting texts (Jonah's Sheol language, burial narratives) are re-absorbed without contradiction once the fish is the devouring ruler and the earth-bars are the foundations of the kingdoms. No supplied text is left unexplained or requires an unsupported step larger than those of the counter.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem as the navel and heart of the land/earth
book_secondary_elaborations: Three days and three nights measure Jesus' time under Jerusalem's custody from arrest (outside the gates) until release on the third day, not merely the tomb interval
Great fish = devouring ruler (Caesar/Rome) governing the sea of peoples
Ship = organized political body of Jerusalem/Judea that surrenders one man so the nation may live

Full scene-by-scene typology of the entire book of Jonah as frame-by-frame Passion prophecy (flight/fare, sleeper, interrogation, innocent blood, casting, gentile worship, anger at mercy to the nations)
Mountains = kingdoms; earth with bars = foundations of those kingdoms under which Jonah/Jesus is held
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading that 'heart of the earth' is simply the tomb/grave (or more broadly Sheol/Hades, the realm of the dead) during the interval between Jesus' death and resurrection, functioning as the direct antitype of Jonah's three days in the fish's belly as a death-confinement image.
counter_core_identification: the tomb/grave or the underworld realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades)
material_core_denial: Denies that the referent is Jerusalem (or any geographic/political center of the land); insists the phrase denotes only the place of burial or the subterranean realm of the dead.
counter_case: Jonah 2:2,6 explicitly equates the fish experience with the belly of Sheol and 'the earth with her bars,' supplying the natural underworld parallel
The sign is presented in the context of death-burial-resurrection (cf. 1 Cor 15:3-4 formula and the burial narratives of Matt 27/Mark 15 etc.)
Parallel descent language elsewhere (Eph 4:9 'lower parts of the earth,' Acts 2:27-31 on not abandoned to Hades, Ps 16:10) is traditionally read as supporting an underworld sojourn
Near-universal Christian consensus and creedal language treat the interval as death-to-resurrection confinement
book_explanatory_advantages: Scripture itself locates the 'midst/navel of the land/earth' as Jerusalem (Ezek 5:5; 38:12), while no text ever calls a grave 'heart of the earth'
Exact linguistic mirror 'heart of the seas' (Jonah 2:3) = heart of the nations yields 'heart of the earth' = heart of the land by the book's own established dictionary
Resolves the three-days-and-three-nights chronology cleanly from arrest to Emmaus-day release without part-day counting or Wednesday-crucifixion proposals
Explains the entire short book of Jonah (not one verse) as the sign Jesus actually cited, producing the dense scene-by-scene Passion match
Integrates the already-accepted Ship symbol (political body) and sea = peoples without remainder
counter_explanatory_advantages: Matches the long-standing consensus reading and requires no novel symbolic dictionary
Directly uses Jonah's own Sheol/earth-bars language as the type
Aligns with the 'buried…raised on the third day' creedal summary and the physical tomb narratives
decisive_sources: Jonah 2:3 (bilvav yammim = heart of the seas)
Jonah 1–4 full narrative with the scene-by-scene Passion table
Prior FULL Ship finding (earthly kingdom/city/state as vessel)
unresolved_objections: Exact hour-count of 'three days and three nights' still depends on a particular reconstruction of the passion chronology (though far less strained than the traditional one)
Traditional spatial readings of Ephesians 4:9 and 1 Peter 3:18-19 are not directly re-engaged in the supplied excerpts
The symbolic method, while internally consistent and previously accepted for Ship, remains a minority hermeneutic
